immaculate

ih-MAK-yuh-lit -- built from the Latin word for 'spot' or 'stain,' with a prefix meaning 'without.' · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Immaculate is perfectly clean and neat, without any flaw or blemish.

The hotel room was immaculate, without a single speck of dust anywhere.

Example

A brand-new car rolls off the showroom floor with an immaculate paint job -- not a single scratch, smudge, or scuff mark anywhere on its surface.

That flawless, spotless condition is exactly what immaculate describes. Unlike 'clean,' which just means free of dirt, immaculate emphasizes total perfection with zero flaws.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

flawless: Flawless means having no imperfections of any kind -- a flawless diamond, argument, or performance. Immaculate is narrower: it praises perfect cleanliness and neatness. A cluttered desk can hold a flawless essay, but only a perfectly clean and ordered room is immaculate.

unblemished: Unblemished means carrying no mark, stain, or scar -- an unblemished apple, an unblemished record. Immaculate goes beyond escaping damage: it describes something actively kept perfectly clean and neat, brought up to a standard rather than merely left unmarked.

tidy: Tidy means neatly arranged, with everything in its place -- but a tidy room can still be dusty. Immaculate demands perfect order and perfect cleanliness together, without a flaw or a speck anywhere, a far higher standard than simply being straightened up.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

filthy: extremely dirty

disheveled: untidy or disordered in appearance

Where it sits · how absolute the perfection is — spotless → immaculate → pristine

spotless vs. immaculate: Spotless is a bit more everyday than immaculate -- spotless usually just means free of visible dirt, while immaculate suggests an almost impossibly perfect, flawless standard of cleanliness.

pristine vs. immaculate: Pristine can feel even more absolute than immaculate: immaculate describes something kept perfectly clean, while pristine implies something completely untouched, as if brand new.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — im-

prefix — im-: not, without (Latin)

root — -macul-

root — -macul-: spot, stain (Latin (macula))

suffix — -ate

suffix — -ate: having, marked by; forms an adjective (Latin (-atus))

Put it together

Put it together: Latin macula meant 'a spot or stain,' and the suffix -ate forms the adjective. Immaculate literally means 'not stained' -- so clean that not a single spot can be found.

Use the root in a new word: maculate

Use the root in a new word: maculate: Unlike its pristine cousin down the hall, the maculate old tablecloth was covered in faded ink stains.
